multipleChoice.question: What tension does the opening discussion establish about eating salt?
options: It is useful for flavour, but its health effects depend mainly on which food contains it.
The body needs some, but many people consume amounts that raise health risks.
It helps the body survive, but a teaspoon is required every day.
It improves ingredients, but its main danger comes from traditional preserved foods.

multipleChoice.question: What does the figure given for Kazakhstan show in relation to the WHO guidance quoted in the programme?
options: The average intake there is only slightly above the guidance.
The average intake there is close to the amount needed for survival.
The average intake there is roughly twice the British recommendation.
The average intake there is more than three times the amount in the WHO guidance.

multipleChoice.question: Why did salting meat become part of the tradition described by the Kazakh interviewee?
options: People had to carry meat while travelling for long periods.
People needed meat to taste stronger than dairy products.
People wanted to replace the milk products they carried.
People had begun to buy more processed food while travelling.

multipleChoice.question: What contrast marks the shift from the historical discussion to modern health concerns?
options: Traditional uses of salt explain why modern processed food is generally safe.
A useful preservation method should determine today's daily intake target.
Salt has had practical value, while high intake today remains a health concern.
Health risks mean the historical value of salting food should be dismissed.

multipleChoice.question: According to the explanation of the body's response, why can excess salt increase strain on the heart?
options: The body releases water, so the heart must replace lost liquid.
Salt directly damages the heart before blood pressure changes.
The body stores less liquid, so blood pressure rises quickly.
The body keeps more water, so the heart pumps more liquid.

multipleChoice.question: How do the Australian and British responses described in the programme differ?
options: Australia restricts food companies; Britain leaves the daily amount for individual consumers to decide.
Australia lowered its daily guidance; Britain also required companies to reduce salt in food.
Australia recommends 5g per day; Britain sets a higher target of 6g for its population.
Australia limits salt in dairy products; Britain directs its restrictions chiefly at traditionally preserved meat.

multipleChoice.question: What is the nutrition professor's main objection to debating whether the limit should be 5g or 6g?
options: It can distract from widespread high intake and its early health consequences.
It gives food companies too little time to change their products.
It overlooks the fact that 1g is the minimum needed for survival.
It assumes every country has exactly the same average intake.

multipleChoice.question: A country has a strong tradition of using salt to preserve food. Which response would best fit the professor's view?
options: Keep the traditional intake because preservation has a useful history.
Set the same exact reduction method used by every other country.
Design a way to address high intake that suits the local culture.
Focus first on settling whether 5g or 6g is the correct number.

multipleChoice.question: What practical purpose do herbs and spices serve in the final advice?
options: They preserve food for longer without changing its taste.
They offer a way to add flavour when using less salt.
They help the body remove water retained after a salty meal.
They make processed food meet the British legal standard.
